p174.lead: Tuesday morning: parting words to each of the twelve, the nature of divine forgiveness, wise answers to trap questions, and the Greeks who came seeking the truth.

p174.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p174.s0.h: Introduction — A Word for Each One
p174.s0.b0: About seven o’clock on Tuesday morning Jesus met the apostles, the women’s corps, and some two dozen other prominent disciples at Simon’s home. He said farewell to Lazarus, giving him the instruction that soon led him to flee to Philadelphia, and he said good-bye to the aged Simon. He also gave his parting advice to the women’s corps, for he never again formally addressed them.
p174.s0.b1: That morning Jesus greeted each of the twelve with a personal salutation. His words go straight to each man’s temperament and to the trial awaiting him. Remembering the very different reactions of the apostles described in the previous paper, we can see how personal these brief charges were.

p174.s0.b3: The word to Peter about weapons and the word to Judas about ridicule connect directly with the events of the preceding papers. Jesus knew of the hidden swords and of the ridicule that had shaken Judas, yet instead of exposing and rebuking them, he offered his counsel as a parting charge.
p174.s0.b4: After these greetings Jesus set out for Jerusalem with Andrew, Peter, James, and John, while the others went to establish the Gethsemane camp, which became their headquarters for the rest of the Master’s life in the flesh. About halfway down Olivet Jesus paused and talked with the four for more than an hour, and from that conversation came his teaching on forgiveness.
p174.s1.h: I. Divine Forgiveness — The Understanding Love of a Parent
p174.s1.b0: Where they had stopped on the slope, Peter asked a question. James held that the Father forgives us even before we ask, while Peter maintained that repentance and confession must come first. Which of them was right? Jesus answered that both erred, because neither grasped the nature of the intimate and loving relations between the creature and the Creator.
p174.s1.b1: Jesus explained with the picture of a wise parent. In a relationship of love and understanding, the very estrangements that would later require repentance and forgiveness never arise. Between the earthly child and the heavenly Father, the divine parent has infinite sympathy and understanding, so divine forgiveness is inevitable, inherent in God himself.

p174.s1.b2.q: It is indeed doubtful whether intelligent and affectionate parents are ever called upon to forgive an average and normal child.

p174.s1.b3.q: Divine justice is so eternally fair that it unfailingly embodies understanding mercy.

p174.s1.b4: A part of every father, Jesus said, lives in the child. The parent sees the child’s immaturity in the light of riper experience and so enjoys a priority of understanding. The same principle holds between people. Whoever understands the inner impulses of his fellows will love them, and this capacity to understand human nature and forgive apparent wrongdoing is Godlike.
p174.s1.b5: Because the child is immature, he often feels a guilty sense of separation from his father’s approval, but the true father is never conscious of any such separation. That is why Jesus said that sin is an experience of creature consciousness, not a part of God’s consciousness. This teaching brings deep comfort to anyone weighed down by guilt.

p174.s1.b6.q: And when you love your brother, you have already forgiven him.

p174.s1.b7: Conversely, an inability or unwillingness to forgive is the measure of our immaturity, and we hold grudges in direct proportion to our ignorance of the inner nature of others. To see forgiveness not merely as an act of will but as a widening of understanding is an insight of great practical use in real relationships.

p174.s1.b8.q: Love is the outworking of the divine and inner urge of life. It is founded on understanding, nurtured by unselfish service, and perfected in wisdom.

p174.s2.h: II–IV. The Trap Questions — Tribute, Resurrection, and the Great Commandment
p174.s2.b0: On Monday evening the Sanhedrin met with some fifty additional leaders chosen from the scribes, Pharisees, and Sadducees. They agreed that arresting Jesus in public was dangerous and that he must first be discredited before the people. So Pharisees, Sadducees, and even Herodians united in a plan to fill the whole day with difficult questions.

p174.s2.b2: To the question of tribute Jesus answered by pointing to the image on the coin. The narrator explains that a well-known ruling of the Sanhedrin already held that the right of coinage carried with it the right to levy taxes. Jesus did not dodge the question; he used the wisdom of a double reply.
p174.s2.b3: Having failed the day before to trip him on ecclesiastical authority, the rulers now tried to entangle him in civil authority. Both Pilate and Herod were in Jerusalem. If he advised against the tribute, they could charge him with sedition before Rome; if he advised paying it, they could alienate the multitude by wounding its national pride. Even the youths who set the trap marveled at his answer.

p174.s2.b4.q: Jesus was never evasive, but he was always wise in his dealings with those who sought to harass and destroy him.

p174.s2.b5: Because the Sadducees accepted only the five Books of Moses, Jesus appealed to Moses alone. He firmly affirmed the survival of mortals through the resurrection, but he did not in any sense endorse the belief in the resurrection of the literal human body. The point he stressed was that God said, “⟦Q 174:3.2⟧I am the God of Abraham,⟦/Q⟧” not “I was.”

p174.s2.b6.q: And so, along with Moses, do I declare that my Father is not the God of the dead but of the living.

p174.s2.b7: The Sadducees aimed not at open persecution but at ridicule, knowing well that public persecution would only win him more sympathy. Yet another group of Sadducees, who had prepared questions about angels, saw what had befallen their comrades and wisely withdrew without a word.
p174.s2.b8: The lawyer who asked about the greatest commandment saw that Jesus had answered in keeping with the highest concept of Jewish religion and openly commended him. Jesus told him he was not far from the kingdom of God, and that very night the man went to the camp near Gethsemane, professed faith in the gospel, and was baptized. Even among those who came to set a trap, there was one whose heart was open to truth.

p174.s2.b9.q: My friend, I perceive that you are not far from the kingdom of God.

p174.s2.b10: Near noon, when no more questions came, Jesus asked one of his own: if the Messiah is the son of David, how can David in the Psalm call him Lord? The rulers never answered, and the narrator records that after Jesus’ death they tried to escape the difficulty by reinterpreting the Psalm or by denying that David wrote it.
p174.s2.b11: The Pharisees had enjoyed the Sadducees’ defeat, and the Sadducees in turn enjoyed the Pharisees’ failure. But the rivalry was only momentary; they soon forgot their time-honored differences in their united effort to stop Jesus. Through it all the common people heard him gladly.
p174.s3.h: V. The Inquiring Greeks — A Grain of Wheat Falls into the Earth
p174.s3.b0: About noon a group of believing Greeks from Alexandria, Athens, and Rome asked Philip to let them see Jesus. Perplexed by the instruction not to teach publicly and by the fact that these men were foreign gentiles, Philip fetched Andrew, and together they brought the Greeks to Joseph’s home. Thirty of these men had decided the night before, at the home of Nicodemus, to enter the kingdom.
p174.s3.b1: With Jews and gentiles gathered in about equal numbers, Jesus perceived the end of one dispensation and the beginning of another. He said he would not sit in judgment on those who rejected him, for he had come not to judge the world but to offer it salvation.
p174.s3.b2: Grieving that the leaders of his people were set on rejecting him, Jesus noted that in that very room were a full score of men who had once sat in the Sanhedrin or the high councils of the nation. Yet some of them still shrank from openly confessing the truth for fear of being cast out of the synagogue. The temptation to love the glory of men more than the glory of God remains a test even for people of faith.

p174.s3.b3.q: except a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it abides alone; but if it dies in good soil, it springs up again to life and bears much fruit.

p174.s3.b4: Jesus confessed that his soul was troubled by the approaching hour, yet he did not pray to be saved from it. Instead he prayed that the Father would glorify his name and that his will be done. Then the Personalized Adjuster who had indwelt him before his baptism appeared and answered; the people heard no voice, but they sensed that an angel had spoken to him.

p174.s3.b5.q: I have glorified my name in your bestowals many times, and I will glorify it once more.

p174.s3.b6: Jesus told them this had happened not for his sake but for theirs, and he urged them to walk in the light while they had it. Then he led them all back to the temple to deliver his farewell discourse.
p174.s4.b0: Paper 174 shows how, amid the tension of the final days, Jesus never lost his calm or his personal care. He left each of the twelve a charge suited to him, explained forgiveness through the understanding love of a parent, and met trap questions with neither evasion nor attack but with wisdom. And facing his approaching death, he chose the Father’s will.

p174.s4.b2: In the next paper, Paper 175, “The Last Temple Discourse,” Jesus gives his final public address in the temple.
p175.lead: The last public discourse in the temple: a hand of mercy held out to the end, an indictment of the leaders’ hypocrisy, and the narrator’s firm warning against prejudice toward individual Jews.

p175.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p175.s0.h: Introduction — The Place of the Last Appeal
p175.s0.b0: Shortly after two o’clock on Tuesday afternoon, Jesus arrived at the temple with eleven apostles, Joseph of Arimathea, the thirty Greeks, and other disciples, and began his last address in its courts. In the morning various groups had questioned him; that afternoon no one asked him anything. The money-changers and merchants had not dared to return since being driven out the day before, and the court was quiet and orderly.
p175.s0.b1: The narrator presents the discourse as having two sides: it was the last appeal to the Jewish people and the final indictment of the religious leaders who sought to destroy him. Before he began, Jesus looked down tenderly on his audience. One thing must be kept in mind throughout this paper: the indictment was aimed not at a whole people but at particular leaders of that day and their practices.
p175.s1.h: I. The Discourse — A Door Left Open to the End
p175.s1.b0: Jesus recalled how long he had proclaimed the Father’s love, and how many had seen the light and entered the kingdom. He and his apostles had done their utmost, in every way consistent with the Father’s will, to live in peace with their brethren and to conform to the reasonable requirements of Moses’ laws and Israel’s traditions. But the leaders would not have peace.

p175.s1.b1.q: Even now it is not too late for this people to receive the word of heaven and to welcome the Son of Man.

p175.s1.b2: The first part of the discourse is closer to invitation than to warning. Jesus said he had offered the joy and liberty of sonship even to the very men who now sought his destruction, and that even now the Father would receive them if they turned to him. At the same time he solemnly warned that if this last chance were rejected, the role of standard-bearer of truth would pass to others.
p175.s1.b3: Jesus said that generation after generation the Father had sent prophets to teach and warn, and that generation after generation these teachers had been rejected. He reminded his hearers that this people had been called to become the light of the world, to show forth the spiritual glory of a God-knowing race. Beneath the rebuke lies respect for that calling and deep sorrow at seeing it cast aside.
p175.s1.b4: He noted that many Jews, Samaritans, and even gentiles had believed the gospel. And he urged the crowd to co-operate with the elders: not to join in any plan to destroy the Son of Man, but in everything related to the peace of Israel to be subject to them and observe the essentials of the law—only not to pattern after their evil works.

p175.s1.b5.q: Remember, this is the sin of these rulers: They say that which is good, but they do it not.

p175.s1.b6: Jesus then restated the principle of humility and service. Call no man Father in the spiritual sense, for there is one Father, God. Do not seek to lord it over your brethren; whoever would be greatest must become the server of all. These words criticize the leaders, but they also hold up a mirror to everyone who hears them.

p175.s1.b7.q: Seek in your daily lives, not self-glorification, but the glory of God.

p175.s2.h: I (continued). The Discourse — An Indictment of Hypocrisy
p175.s2.b0: Before his indictment Jesus made it plain that he bore no malice toward the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees. He knew too that many in his audience believed in secret and would openly profess their allegiance when his hour came. What he challenged was not persons but an attitude: professing to talk with God while rejecting the one who came to reveal the Father.

p175.s2.b1.q: I bear no malice toward these chief priests and rulers who even now seek my destruction

p175.s2.b3: The figure of the cup and the platter yields the most practical lesson of the whole indictment: cleanse the inside first, and what spills over will of itself cleanse the outside. The danger of conforming outward performance to the letter of the law while neglecting the soul belongs to every religion and every age.
p175.s2.b4: Most of the charges aim at the gap between outside and inside: piety performed to be seen, scrupulous attention to small rules while mercy and faith are neglected, and the contradiction of adorning the prophets’ tombs while rejecting present truth. When Jesus said that if the blind lead the blind both will fall into the pit, he was warning that a leader’s hypocrisy ends by harming those who follow.

p175.s2.b5.q: Do you not recognize how much better it would be first to cleanse the inside of the cup, and then that which spills over would of itself cleanse the outside?

p175.s2.b6: Yet even at the end of these severe words, Jesus held out mercy once more. Even now, he said, he offered mercy and forgiveness in the Father’s name and proffered the loving hand of eternal fellowship. Then he lamented that he would have gathered Jerusalem’s children as a hen gathers her chickens, but they would not; he declared that his work in the temple was done and beckoned his followers to depart.
p175.s3.h: II. Status of Individual Jews — The Narrator’s Solemn Charge
p175.s3.b0: Immediately after recording the discourse, the narrator stops the story to address the reader directly. The fact that certain spiritual leaders and religious teachers of that time rejected Jesus and conspired to bring about his death does not in any way affect the standing of any individual Jew before God. This section is the key to reading the whole paper rightly.

p175.s3.b1.q: And it should not cause those who profess to be followers of the Christ to be prejudiced against the Jew as a fellow mortal.

p175.s3.b2: The narrator reminds us that Jesus himself was a Jew by natural birth, and that those who first accepted his gospel and died for its truth—Peter, Philip, Matthew, and others—were Palestinian Jews. He goes so far as to say that a shudder of horror passes over the onlooking celestial beings when professed followers of Jesus persecute these men’s descendants.

p175.s3.b4.q: The Father and his Creator Son have never ceased to love the Jews.

p175.s3.b5: The charge exposes the contradiction of justifying hatred in the name of one who taught his disciples to love even their enemies. The lesson for the reader is clear: no group or individual today may be condemned on the basis of a scene from history, for God is no respecter of persons.
p175.s4.h: III–IV. The Fateful Sanhedrin Meeting and the Night in Jerusalem
p175.s4.b0: At eight o’clock that evening the Sanhedrin was called to order. It had informally decreed his death before, but it had never resolved to arrest him and bring about his death at any and all costs. Just before midnight it voted unanimously to impose the death sentence on both Jesus and Lazarus, ordering that Jesus be taken early the next morning but not in public—in secret, preferably suddenly and at night.

p175.s4.b1.q: The passing of death sentence (even before his trial) upon the Son of God was the Sanhedrin’s reply to the last offer of heavenly mercy ever to be extended to the Jewish nation, as such.

p175.s4.b2: The narrator interprets this decision as the Sanhedrin’s reply to the last offer of heavenly mercy extended to the nation as such, and says that from then on the nation was left to finish its national life on a purely human footing among the nations. This is a statement about the nation as a sociopolitical group, and, as the preceding section stressed, it is distinct from the spiritual standing of any individual.

Why they wanted Jesus removed

p175.s4.b4: The Sanhedrin adjourned near midnight, agreeing to meet at ten the next morning at the home of Caiaphas the high priest to formulate the charges. A small group of Sadducees actually proposed assassination, but the Pharisees utterly refused to countenance it. The narrator fairly records that even within the opposing camp there was a line some would not cross.
p175.s4.b5: Judas did not hear the merciful first half of the discourse; he had been conferring with Sadducean relatives and friends about how best to break away from the apostles. Listening to the indictment in the second half, he finally and fully made up his mind to forsake the gospel movement. Meanwhile, at the home of Nicodemus, more than thirty prominent Jews who believed in secret agreed to declare their allegiance openly the moment they heard of his arrest.

p175.s4.b6.q: All present agreed that they would make open acknowledgment of their allegiance to the Master in the very hour they should hear of his arrest. And that is just what they did.

p175.s4.b7: That night, while all Jerusalem buzzed with the question “⟦Q 175:4.2⟧What will they do with Jesus?⟦/Q⟧”, a vast concourse of celestial beings hovered over the scene, longing to help their beloved Sovereign but restrained by their commanding superiors from acting.
p175.s5.b0: Paper 175 contains some of the sternest words Jesus ever spoke, yet they are framed on both sides by mercy. He indicted without malice, and after indicting he held out his hand again. And the narrator insists that this scene must never be used to justify hatred of any people or person. To read this paper rightly is to take its warning against hypocrisy not as a story about others but as an occasion for self-examination.

p175.s5.b2: In the next paper, Paper 176, “Tuesday Evening on Mount Olivet,” Jesus speaks to the apostles about the future of Jerusalem and about his second coming.
p176.lead: The temple that would fall and the Lord who would return: prophecy under the moon on Olivet, the parable of the talents, and the right attitude toward Michael’s return.

p176.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p176.s0.h: Introduction — A Question Asked While Looking at the Temple
p176.s0.b0: On Tuesday afternoon, as they left the temple, Matthew pointed to its massive stones and beautiful adornment and asked whether such buildings could really be destroyed. Jesus answered that not one stone would be left upon another. The apostles could conceive of no event short of the end of the world that could bring about the temple’s destruction. This paper shows how these two ideas—the fate of Jerusalem and the end of the world—became tangled in the apostles’ minds.
p176.s0.b1: To avoid the crowds, the group climbed a little way up the western slope of Olivet and looked down on the temple glowing in the setting sun. When they had sat down under the full moon, Nathaniel asked how they would know when these things were about to happen. With that question the long teaching of the evening began.
p176.s0.b2: The paper has four sections: the destruction of Jerusalem, the Master’s second coming, the later discussion at the camp with the parable of the talents, and the narrator’s own account of the return of Michael. As we read, it is important to hold two questions apart. One concerns a historical catastrophe soon to fall on a single city; the other concerns a visit, at a time no one knows, by the sovereign of a universe. The apostles’ confusion came from merging the two.
p176.s1.h: I. The Destruction of Jerusalem — When to Flee
p176.s1.b0: Jesus first warned them not to be deceived. Many would come claiming to be deliverers, and wars, famines, and earthquakes would not themselves mean that the end had come. The apostles would be thrown out of the synagogue, imprisoned, even betrayed by their own kinsfolk, but when they stood before judges, the spirit would teach them what to say.

p176.s1.b1.q: but even in these persecutions I will not forsake you; my spirit will not desert you.

p176.s1.b2: The narrator names the cause of Jerusalem’s fall plainly: the rejection of the spiritual concept of the Messiah and the blind determination to cling to a material deliverer would bring the Jews into direct conflict with the Roman armies. Because Jerusalem was to be the cradle of the early gospel movement, Jesus did not want its teachers and preachers to perish in the coming revolts, and so he gave specific instructions.

p176.s1.b4: Because of this warning, practically all the believers fled to Pella in the north when the Roman troops first appeared. Yet many followers took the prediction to refer to the New Jerusalem and the end of the world. Jesus lamented that they always erred because they tried to attach the new teaching to the old.
p176.s1.b5: The scene shows the practical value of a warning. The prophecy was meant not to frighten but to help people avoid harm that could be avoided. At the same time, settled beliefs will bend even the plainest words to fit their own frame. Readers may ask whether they, too, are fitting the teachings they hear into conclusions they already wanted.
p176.s2.h: II. The Master’s Second Coming — An Evening of Two Tangled Subjects
p176.s2.b0: Jesus had more than once implied that he would leave and yet return, and the apostles promptly tied that promise to the destruction of Jerusalem. He reminded them again that his kingdom was not of this world, and that what was now ending would be a new beginning, out of which the gospel would go to all the world. Meanwhile his Spirit of Truth would comfort and guide them.

p176.s2.b1.q: You behold me now in weakness and in the flesh, but when I return, it shall be with power and in the spirit.

p176.s2.b2: The time of his return, he said, is known only in the councils of Paradise. But as the fig tree’s tender leaves tell us that summer is near, so after the long winter of material-mindedness they should discern the spiritual springtime of a new dispensation. Then he connected the teaching with each person’s death: what the whole world faces at the end of an age, each individual faces as a personal experience at the end of life.

p176.s2.b4: The narrator says that no discourse ever became so confused in the apostles’ minds as this one. The later written accounts did not agree, and a Jewish apocalyptic written by one Selta was even copied into the Gospel records; the parable of the ten virgins first appeared in those writings. The Apostle John, however, never became thus confused.
p176.s2.b5: Jesus also reminded them that the Father had already sent several bestowals to this dark world: the one who became the prince of darkness, then Adam, then Melchizedek, and in these days the Son of Man. The promise of an enlarged revelation of truth when the kingdom comes to full fruition offers a view in which revelation is not a single event but continues age after age. Seen this way, his return is less a dreadful end than one more scene in the Father’s ongoing mercy.
p176.s2.b6: The thirteen walked toward the camp in silence. On this very road Judas finally confirmed his decision to abandon his associates. Though it was late, the apostles did not want to sleep; they wanted to hear more about Jerusalem, the Master’s departure, and the end of the world.
p176.s3.h: III. Later Discussion at the Camp — The Parable of the Talents
p176.s3.b0: Late that night, with some twenty gathered around the campfire, Thomas asked what their attitude should be while the Master was away on the Father’s business. Jesus answered that their connection with the kingdom was wholly spiritual and personal. The fall of nations, the end of an age, even the end of the world—none of these could seriously concern one who had hidden his life in the eternal kingdom.

p176.s3.b1.q: Kingdom builders, the accredited citizens of the heavenly worlds, are not to be disturbed by temporal upheavals or perturbed by terrestrial cataclysms.

p176.s3.b2: But Jesus quickly added a warning. Survival faith is a living faith that bears ever more fruit of the spirit. Having once accepted sonship will not save one who knowingly and persistently refuses to bear that fruit. Then he told the parable of the master who, before a long journey, entrusted his goods to his servants.

p176.s3.b3.q: this survival faith is a living faith, and it increasingly manifests the fruits of that divine spirit which first inspired it in the human heart.

p176.s3.b4: Jesus compared waiting for his return to the way we face death. Just as each believer carries on his lifework in view of an inevitable and ever-impending natural death, so each generation should carry on its work in view of the Son of Man’s possible return. The comparison frees belief about the end from fear and excitement and turns it into a calm, steady, everyday responsibility.

p176.s3.b6.q: You cannot stand still in the affairs of the eternal kingdom.

p176.s3.b7: The narrator extends the parable to the stewardship of truth. Truth is living, so to boast of having preserved what was entrusted in fixed form, changing nothing, is merely an excuse for spiritual indolence. And the one-talent servant who blamed his failure on his master is like every selfish mortal who puts the blame for his own failures on others.
p176.s3.b8: It matters that this parable is an answer to the question about the second coming. The servants could not know when their lord would return. What was asked of them was not to predict the date but to make gains with what they had been given. In the next world we will give account of our endowments and stewardships, and whether our talents are few or many, the reckoning will be just and merciful. The right way to await his return, then, is faithful service day by day.

p176.s3.b9.q: Truth is living; the Spirit of Truth is ever leading the children of light into new realms of spiritual reality and divine service.

p176.s3.b10.q: Freely have you received; therefore freely should you give of the truth of heaven

p176.s4.h: IV. The Return of Michael — What We Know and What We Do Not
p176.s4.b0: No part of the Master’s teaching has been so misunderstood as his promise to return. His followers first connected it with the fall of Jerusalem, and when the temple fell and still he did not appear, they connected it with the end of the age and even the end of the world. The narrator sets out the two things Jesus promised to do after his ascension.

head: Promise
What the narrator makes clear
rows: The first promise
To send another teacher, the Spirit of Truth — fulfilled on the day of Pentecost
The second promise
To return personally to this world someday — without saying how, where, or when
What many of the narrators believe

What is certain

p176.s4.b2.q: You would do well, therefore, to disassociate the Master’s personal return to earth from any and all set events or settled epochs.

p176.s4.b3: The narrator says that the second advent has great sentimental value, but for human beings it is of no more practical importance than natural death, which brings us directly into the presence of the sovereign of our universe. Whether we go to him or he comes to us first is of no serious concern.
p176.s4.b4: In this section the narrator honestly separates what is known from what is not. Urantia will forever be one of the seven nativity spheres of Michael, and among his titles he carries that of Planetary Prince of Urantia, so it is natural that he should wish to return. Yet whether that will be with the judgment of this age, at the close of some later age, or as an unannounced, isolated event, the narrator says plainly that he does not know. This willingness to say “⟦Q 176:4.5⟧we do not know⟦/Q⟧” is the soundest antidote to the endless speculation surrounding the second coming.

p176.s4.b5.q: Be you therefore ever ready to welcome him on earth as he stands ready to welcome you in heaven.

p176.s5.b0: To those who ask for a timetable of the end, Paper 176 offers an attitude instead. About the destruction of Jerusalem Jesus gave a specific way of escape, but about the time of his return he said that no one knows. What he asked instead was that we increase what has been entrusted to us and live ready to welcome him at any time. From this paper readers can learn a faith that stands firm even amid unsettling news of the times.

p176.s5.b2: In the next paper, Paper 177, “Wednesday, the Rest Day,” Jesus spends a day in the hills with John Mark, and Judas at last strikes his bargain of betrayal.
p177.lead: The last quiet day on earth: a day in the hills with John Mark, a talk on home life, and Judas’s visit that same day to the house of Caiaphas.

p177.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p177.s0.b0: When the work of teaching did not press them, Jesus and his apostles rested from their labors every Wednesday. On this Wednesday morning an ominous silence hung over the camp. Jesus told the apostles to rest, to think over everything that had happened since they came to Jerusalem, and to meditate on what lay just ahead. He added only one restriction: under no circumstances were they to go within the gates of the city.

p177.s0.b1.q: Make sure that the truth abides in your lives, and that you daily grow in grace.

p177.s0.b2: This paper records two people who went in opposite directions on the same day. A boy went up into the hills with the Master and spent the day in fellowship with God; an apostle ignored the Master’s request, went down into the city, and agreed to hand him over. Between them, the remaining apostles endured a day without their Master and passed through the lowest point of their discouragement. This contrast is the key to reading the whole paper.

p177.s1.h: I. One Day Alone with God — The Boy Who Would Not Let Go of the Basket
p177.s1.b0: When Jesus made ready to go into the hills alone, David Zebedee wanted to send three armed men with him. Jesus declined the escort: no man would lay hands on him until the hour when he was ready to lay down his life in conformity to his Father’s will. Then John Mark came forward with a small basket of food and water.
p177.s1.b1: As Jesus reached down to take the basket, the boy held on to it and said that if he came along to carry the lunch, the Master would be more free to worship. He even promised to be silent and ask no questions. His boldness astonished some who stood near, but Jesus saw the whole heart of the lad and took him along.

p177.s1.b2.q: Since with all your heart you crave to go with me, it shall not be denied you.

p177.s1.b3.q: Forever this occasion exemplifies the willingness of the Creator to fellowship the creature.

p177.s1.b4: What stands out in this scene is not the boy’s qualifications but his desire. John Mark regretted that he had not been old enough to be one of the apostles. Yet he had followed the group almost constantly since their first preaching at the Jordan ford near Jericho, and that steady love led to this day’s companionship. It is a comfort to every reader that fellowship with God is open not according to rank or age but according to the longing of the heart.
p177.s1.b5: This day became known on high as “⟦Q 177:1.3⟧the day which a young man spent with God in the hills.⟦/Q⟧” The text says that even a youth, if the desire of the heart is really supreme, can command the attention and enjoy the loving companionship of the God of a universe. Jesus told the lad not to become discouraged by impending events and assured him he would live to become a mighty messenger of the kingdom. John Mark never revealed what he heard that day, and in the hours that remained he never let the Master out of his sight for long.
p177.s2.h: II. Early Home Life — Love Ruled by Wisdom
p177.s2.b0: Much of the day’s conversation was spent comparing the childhood of the two. When John asked how he could know he would become a mighty messenger of the kingdom, Jesus pointed to his home as the ground on which his faith and love could be relied upon: parents who bore each other a sincere affection, and parents who possessed wisdom as well as love.

head: What John Mark’s home avoided
What he enjoyed instead
rows: Being overloved so that his sense of self-importance was injuriously exalted
A parental love that insures laudable self-confidence and fosters normal feelings of security
Parents maneuvering against each other for the child’s confidence and loyalty
Parents who bore each other a sincere affection
The indulgences and luxuries that wealth can buy
The synagogue school, along with his neighborhood playfellows
Having to wound love in order to gain independence
Learning how to live by being permitted original experience

p177.s2.b2: Jesus offered John’s friend Amos as a contrast. Amos’s parents loved their son so much that they refused to let him come along. Amos believed the gospel just as much as John, yet Jesus said he could not fully depend on him, because his early home life was not such as would produce a wholly dependable person. John, by contrast, had spent his first eight years in a home where love prevailed and wisdom reigned, and so he had the kind of loyalty that would go through to the end.

p177.s2.b3.q: When you get married and have children of your own to rear, make sure that your love is admonished by wisdom and guided by intelligence.

p177.s2.b4: Jesus explained that a child depends almost entirely on the home for his early concepts of everything intellectual, social, moral, and even spiritual. The child gets his first impressions of the universe from the mother’s care and his first ideas of the heavenly Father from the earthly father. The narrator adds that the gospel, founded as it is on the father-child relationship, can hardly enjoy world-wide acceptance until home life embraces more of love and more of wisdom. Modern homes have gained freedom, he notes, but that liberty is not restrained by love, motivated by loyalty, or directed by the intelligent discipline of wisdom.

p177.s2.b5.q: Such a home life enhances religion, and genuine religion always glorifies the home.

p177.s3.h: III. The Day at Camp — The Empty Place
p177.s3.b0: The apostles walked about visiting the disciples’ tents, but by afternoon they were anxious for the Master’s safety and felt inexpressibly lonely without him. No one said so openly, yet every one of them except Judas wished himself in John Mark’s place. Nathaniel spoke to a few of them on “Supreme Desire” and confessed that their trouble was that they were halfhearted. His remark that only the boy who would not let go of the basket went with the Master sums up the lesson of this paper: the strength of desire determines the companionship.

p177.s3.b1.q: What is wrong with most of us is that we are only halfhearted.

p177.s3.b2: Meanwhile David Zebedee, convinced that the rulers were going to kill Jesus, had sent for his mother and asked her to bring Mary and every member of Jesus’ family to Jerusalem. Because he had done this on his own initiative, he told no one. More than twenty of the Greeks who had met Jesus at the home of Joseph of Arimathea also came to the camp. Jesus visited with them that evening, and had it not been for the disturbance it would have caused his apostles, he would have ordained them as he had the seventy. In the city, the chief priests wondered why Jesus did not return to the temple, while they prepared for the Passover and perfected their plans to destroy him.
p177.s4.h: IV. Judas and the Chief Priests — Not Money, but a Wounded Self
p177.s4.b0: Shortly after Jesus and John Mark left, Judas ignored the Master’s request and hurried to the home of Caiaphas. An informal meeting of the Sanhedrin was being held there to decide on the charges against Jesus and the procedure for securing Roman confirmation of his death sentence. The day before, Judas had told relatives and Sadducean friends that Jesus was a well-meaning dreamer but not the deliverer of Israel, and they had flattered him with the promise of high honors.
p177.s4.b1: The text examines Judas’s motives layer by layer and states plainly that he did not go to Caiaphas for money. Introduced by his cousin, Judas asked the high priest what he would give for this service, and he failed to notice the disdain on Caiaphas’s face. They agreed to arrest Jesus on Thursday night, after the pilgrims had retired.

How the text describes it

Resentment at being unrecognized

p177.s4.b3.q: the other apostles likewise craved this same worldly honor in their minds, but with their hearts they loved Jesus and were doing their best to learn to love the truths which he taught them.

p177.s4.b4: This passage weighs heavily precisely because it does not paint Judas as a monster. The early ambition was shared by all the apostles. The difference lay in whether that ambition was overcome by love in the heart or fed by disappointment and resentment. Once Judas separated himself from the support of his brethren and exposed himself to the insinuations of his enemies, the long-accumulated wounds were ready to engulf him. Here the reader may take warning about how small, unresolved hurts can grow.
p177.s4.b5: Judas returned to camp intoxicated with thoughts of grandeur such as he had not had for many a day. He rejoiced that he had been shrewd enough to trade the glory he failed to win in the new kingdom for honor and reward in the old order. The text judges that, in its last motive of conscious intention, his betrayal was the cowardly act of a selfish deserter who thought only of his own safety and glory. Jesus loved and trusted Judas just as he did the other apostles, but Judas failed to return that trust with love. The chief priests now had a way to take Jesus without arresting him in public.

p177.s4.b6.q: And every mortal man knows full well how love, even when once genuine, can, through disappointment, jealousy, and long-continued resentment, be eventually turned into actual hate.

p177.s5.h: V. The Last Social Hour — Beware the Support of the Multitude
p177.s5.b0: Wednesday evening was a social hour, but the apostles could not be cheered. Jesus asked carefully about each of their families, and David Zebedee looked down at his feet, afraid to answer. On this occasion Jesus warned them not to be deceived by the crowds in the temple who seemed to believe their teaching. Those who know the gospel only in the mind and have not experienced it in the heart cannot be depended on when real trouble comes.

p177.s5.b1.q: Watch, therefore, and pray that on the morrow you may be strengthened for the days that are just ahead.

p177.s5.b2: The text records this Wednesday evening as the low-tide mark of the apostles’ spiritual status up to the hour of the Master’s death. Even his good cheer frightened them. Just before midnight, knowing this was the last night he would sleep through with his chosen family, Jesus sent them to rest and called the coming day one more day to do the Father’s will.
p177.s6.b0: Paper 177 shows how far human choices can diverge within a single quiet day. Among those who followed the same Master, a boy stood beside him out of longing, and an apostle left him out of resentment. The teaching on the home reminds us how early the roots of such a parting are laid. Readers can examine both the warmth of their own desire and any resentment stored in their hearts.

p177.s6.b2: In the next paper, Paper 178, “Last Day at the Camp,” Jesus spends Thursday with his apostles and prepares for the Last Supper.
p178.lead: The last free day on earth: a farewell discourse on sonship in the heavenly kingdom and citizenship in earthly governments, and the road to the upper room.

p178.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p178.s0.b0: Jesus planned this Thursday as his last free day on earth as a divine Son incarnated in the flesh. After breakfast he led the apostles and a few loyal disciples to a secluded spot above the camp and taught them many new truths. This forenoon talk was his farewell address to the whole camp group, both Jews and gentiles.
p178.s0.b1: Only Judas was missing. Some of the apostles supposed the Master had sent him into the city on an errand, probably to arrange the Passover. He did not return until midafternoon. The paper falls into three parts: in the morning, the discourse on citizenship; in the afternoon, the preparation of the supper and David Zebedee’s quiet activity; and toward evening, the last words on the way down into the city.
p178.s1.h: I. Sonship and Citizenship (1) — Living in Two Kingdoms at Once
p178.s1.b0: For almost two hours Jesus talked with about fifty of his trusted followers and answered a score of questions about the relation of the kingdom of heaven to the kingdoms of this world. The narrator summarizes the discourse in modern language. Its core is this: the kingdoms of this world are material and may need physical force, but the kingdom of heaven is a spiritual brotherhood of spirit-born sons and may be promulgated only by the power of the spirit.

p178.s1.b2: Jesus said there is nothing incompatible between the two requirements. Conflict arises only if a Caesar usurps the prerogatives of God and demands supreme worship. Even then, the believer should worship only God while seeking to enlighten such misguided rulers. Sonship in the kingdom should instead make one a better citizen, and the believer, besides his duty to man and his duty to God, voluntarily assumes a third obligation: service to the brotherhood of believers.

p178.s1.b3.q: The fruits of the spirit, your sincere and loving service, are the mighty social lever to uplift the races of darkness, and this Spirit of Truth will become your power-multiplying fulcrum.

p178.s1.b4: He urged them to show wisdom and sagacity in dealing with unbelieving rulers: to iron out minor disagreements with discretion and, in everything short of their spiritual allegiance to the rulers of the universe, to live peaceably with all men. He also foretold that while rulers acted as religious dictators, believers could expect persecution, yet the light they bore and the very manner of their suffering would eventually bring about the gradual divorcement of politics and religion.

p178.s1.b5.q: Be you always as wise as serpents but as harmless as doves.

p178.s1.b6.q: Learn to be faithful to the kingdom even in times of peace and prosperity.

p178.s1.b7: This warning is surprisingly sharp. More dangerous than times of persecution are the times when most men speak well of believers and many in high places nominally accept the gospel. Believers are to keep watch on their own, so that the angels need not lead their ease-drifting souls into troublous ways. For today’s reader, the passage raises the question whether comfort is dulling one’s faith.
p178.s2.h: I. Sonship and Citizenship (2) — Preaching the Gospel and Serving
p178.s2.b0: Jesus told them never to let anything divert their devotion to the one duty of preaching the gospel. Loving spiritual ministry, enlightening intellectual communion, and uplifting social service should overflow to all mankind, but none of these, nor all of them together, may take the place of proclaiming the gospel. Such ministries are the social by-products of the more sublime transformation wrought in the believer’s heart.

p178.s2.b1.q: Whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do even so to them.

p178.s2.b2: He told them to persuade, never to compel, and never to promote truth through the power of civil government or secular law. A believer in public service must not be a poorer civil servant than an unbeliever; if he is, he should ask whether the roots of truth in his heart have died. Jesus then set side by side what believers must not be and what they should be.
p178.s2.b3: Underneath this teaching lies the consciousness of sonship with God. Jesus said that this consciousness should quicken the entire life service of every man, woman, and child. Faith is not meant to make people neglect their work and public duties; it should be a mighty stimulus that awakens the powers lying within the personality. Since faithfulness at work is itself a fruit of faith, this teaching applies directly to any ordinary working person.

p178.s2.b5: After the leaven and the mustard seed, Jesus compared the gospel to the seed of the living being, which remains the same seed while it unfolds in new manifestations from generation to generation, adapting to the needs of each age. He did not want the gospel to become merely a sacred memory or tradition. He also told the apostles not to attack the old ways, but skillfully to put the leaven of new truth in the midst of the old beliefs.
p178.s2.b6: Jesus recalled that he and the apostles had never directly attacked the persons or the authority of those who sit in Moses’ seat. They had only offered new light, and they clashed with the leaders only when those leaders blocked the preaching of the gospel. Even now, it was the leaders who were the attackers. Yet when the willful unbeliever attacks, they were to defend vigorously the truth that had saved them. Here gentleness and courage go together in balance.

p178.s2.b7.q: From generation to generation this gospel must show increasing vitality and exhibit greater depth of spiritual power.

p178.s2.b8.q: Show yourselves to be loyal citizens, upright artisans, praiseworthy neighbors, devoted kinsmen, understanding parents, and sincere believers in the brotherhood of the Father’s kingdom.

p178.s3.h: II. After the Noontide Meal — An Upper Room Quietly Prepared
p178.s3.b0: Not many took in the forenoon address; the Greeks understood it best. Even the apostles could not reconcile the Master’s references to future political kingdoms and successive generations of believers with his impending death. By noon everyone had heard of Lazarus’s hasty flight from Bethany.
p178.s3.b1: Through his secret agents, David Zebedee knew all about the plot, including Judas’s part in it. When he began to ask the Master whether he knew, Jesus raised his hand and stopped him: he knew all about it. David was to tell no one and was not to doubt that the will of God would prevail in the end. When word came asking whether Abner of Philadelphia should come to Jerusalem, Jesus sent back the message to go on with his work.

p178.s3.b2.q: If I depart from you in the flesh, it is only that I may return in the spirit.

p178.s3.b3: When Philip asked about the Passover, Jesus called Peter and John. As Judas drew near to overhear, David engaged him in conversation and kept him occupied. Jesus told the three to follow a man bearing a water pitcher whom they would meet at the city gate. All this had been arranged with John Mark the day before in the hills, because if Judas learned the place in advance, the supper might be disturbed. That same day Judas turned over all the apostolic money to David.

p178.s4.h: III. On the Way to the Supper — Looking Down on the City
p178.s4.b0: About half past four Jesus set out with the twelve. This was the last journey he ever made with all twelve of them. When they reached the place where he had spoken the evening before about the destruction of Jerusalem, they unconsciously paused and looked down on the city. Since Jesus did not wish to pass through the city until after sunset, he spoke his last words to them there.

p178.s4.b1.q: As the Father sent me into this world, so am I about to send you forth to represent me and finish the work I have begun.

p178.s4.b2: These words carry the weight of the past years. The apostles had been witnesses of the experience of being laborers together with God, and Jesus had long warned them that he must leave. He had set them apart in the hills of Capernaum precisely so that they could carry on the work after he was gone. Now they had to make ready to share with others the experience they had had with him.

p178.s4.b3.q: I need no defense by the hand of man; the armies of heaven are even now near at hand

p178.s4.b4: He told them not to expose themselves needlessly to peril by any foolish attempt to defend him. Just as Lazarus had been sent away to safety, the apostles must live to witness to the gospel. And when they saw the city destroyed, they were not to forget that they had already entered upon the eternal life of endless service. In the Father’s universe there are many abodes, and when they had finished their work on earth, they too would come to the Master’s joy.
p178.s4.b5: As they entered the city through the narrow streets in the gathering darkness, no one in the crowds recognized that the Son of God was passing by. Only three of the apostles knew where they were going, and none of them knew that one of their own number had already entered into a conspiracy to betray the Master. John Mark followed them to the gate, then ran ahead by another street to welcome them at his home.
p178.s5.b0: Paper 178 shows the teaching of Jesus on the eve of his death reaching beyond personal salvation to the life of the believer in society and the state. Jesus did not tell believers to turn their backs on the world, nor to spread their faith by borrowing worldly power. Instead he showed how a person living by the spirit becomes the best citizen, neighbor, and parent. At the same time, with danger approaching, he calmly prepared the supper and trusted the Father’s will.

p179.lead: The upper room in John Mark’s home: amid a quarrel over seats, the Master kneels to wash their feet, makes a last appeal to the betrayer, and leaves the supper of remembrance.

p179.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p179.s0.h: Introduction — A Passover One Day Early
p179.s0.b0: Since the Jews reckoned the day as beginning at sunset, the regular Passover supper was due to be eaten on Friday night. Yet Jesus gathered his apostles on Thursday evening. They did not fully understand why. Some thought he knew he would be arrested before Friday; others took it as a special occasion preceding the regular Passover.
p179.s0.b1: There was no lamb at this supper. The apostles knew that Jesus did not personally take part in any sacrificial service of the Jewish system, and that when he was the host no lamb was ever served. It had also been arranged beforehand that only the twelve would be present, so no servants were provided. This small fact sets the first scene of the evening.

p179.s1.h: I. The Desire for Preference — The Basin No One Picked Up
p179.s1.b0: As the apostles entered the upper room, they saw the pitchers of water, the basins, and the towels just inside the door. With no servant present, each wondered who would wash their feet, and each thought it would not be he. Then they surveyed the seating at the table. Judas stepped over to the seat of honor at the left of the host, and John Zebedee claimed the place on the right.
p179.s1.b1: Peter, enraged, marched clear around the table and took the lowest couch. The text is candid about his motive. It was not only a protest; he hoped that Jesus would see him in the place of least honor, call him up to a higher one, and displace someone who had presumed to honor himself. This scene holds up a mirror to the reader: even an act that looks humble can hide a desire for position.
p179.s1.b2: The seating was finally settled: John on the Master’s right, Judas on his left, then Simon Zelotes, Matthew, James Zebedee, Andrew, the Alpheus twins, Philip, Nathaniel, Thomas, and at the very end Simon Peter. The narrator reminds us that they had gathered to celebrate an institution older than Moses, recalling the time when their fathers were slaves in Egypt. At a feast of liberation, they had made themselves slaves to the love of honor.

p179.s1.b3.q: even in such a solemn setting, under the leadership of Judas the apostles are led once more to give way to their old predilection for honor, preference, and personal exaltation.

p179.s1.b4: While they were still exchanging angry recriminations, the Master appeared in the doorway. He hesitated a moment as a look of disappointment slowly crept over his face, but without comment he went to his place and did not disturb their seating. Their feet were still unwashed, and the mood in the room was anything but pleasant.
p179.s2.h: II. Beginning the Supper — Only One Anxiety
p179.s2.b0: After a few moments of silence, Jesus relieved the tension with a smile. He told them he had wanted to eat with them once more before he suffered, and that the morrow was in the Father’s hands. After giving thanks over the first cup, he said he would not again drink the fruit of the vine with them until they sat down together in the kingdom to come.

p179.s2.b1.q: as concerns the morrow, we are all in the hands of the Father, whose will I have come to execute.

p179.s2.b2: The text here discloses the Master’s inner life. He knew he had revealed the Father’s love, shown forth his mercy, and completed what he came into the world to do. He knew too that Judas’s betrayal also pleased Lucifer, Satan, and Caligastia. But he feared neither those who sought his physical death nor those who sought his spiritual overthrow. His one anxiety was for the safety and salvation of his chosen followers.
p179.s3.h: III. Washing the Apostles’ Feet — The One Who Serves Is the Greatest
p179.s3.b0: After the first cup, the Master quietly rose, removed his outer garment, girded himself with a towel, and poured water into a basin. He went to the lowest seat, where Peter reclined, and knelt in the attitude of a servant. All twelve rose as one man; even Judas for a moment forgot himself in astonishment.
p179.s3.b1: Peter, the first to believe wholeheartedly in Jesus’ divinity and to confess it publicly, could not bear to see his Master wash his feet like a slave. He refused outright. But when he heard that unless he accepted this service he would have no part in the Master’s work, he impulsively asked him to wash his hands and head as well. Judas, on the other hand, read this humility as proof that Jesus would never qualify as Israel’s deliverer and concluded that his own decision was right.

p179.s3.b3: In silence Jesus went around the table and washed the feet of all twelve, not even passing by Judas. Then he returned to his place and asked them: if the Master has washed your feet, why were you unwilling to wash one another’s feet? Why, he asked, were they so slow to learn that the secret of greatness in the spiritual kingdom is not like the methods of power in the material world?

p179.s3.b4.q: But why are you so slow to learn that the secret of greatness in the spiritual kingdom is not like the methods of power in the material world?

p179.s3.b5.q: He who would be great among you, let him become as the younger; while he who would be chief, let him become as one who serves.

p179.s3.b6.q: But you will observe that I am among you as one who serves.

p179.s3.b7: The Master said there could be no place of preferment at his table, for he loved each of them as he did the others. The place nearest him, as men regard such honors, meant nothing concerning their standing in the kingdom of heaven. The teaching still questions every community today. What shows a community’s spiritual level is not who sits in front, but who picks up the basin first.
p179.s4.h: IV. Last Words to the Betrayer — The Sop
p179.s4.b0: When the meal had become cheerful again, Jesus explained that, knowing of the plot against him, he had chosen to eat this supper a day early in this secret chamber. He said that his going to the Father was necessary, but it was not required that one of them should betray him. Disconcerted, they all asked, “⟦Q 179:4.2⟧Is it I?⟦/Q⟧”

p179.s4.b1.q: How deceitful is the intellectual pride that precedes the spiritual downfall!

p179.s4.b2: John leaned toward the Master and asked who it was, and Peter urged John across the table to find out. Jesus had already said plainly that it was the one to whom he gave the sop, yet they did not grasp it. Only Judas was painfully conscious of the meaning, and he feared that his brethren now knew him for the betrayer. The same words passed over those who loved the Master and pierced the one who was hiding his heart.
p179.s4.b3: Dipping the bread in the dish of herbs, Jesus handed it to Judas on his left, saying, “⟦Q 179:4.3⟧You have said.⟦/Q⟧” Since it was natural for the host to give a sop to the guest on his left, the others noticed nothing. Jesus said he sorrowed that this evil had come to pass and had hoped up to this hour that truth might triumph over the deceptions of evil. Then, leaning toward Judas, he told him to do quickly what he had decided to do, and Judas went out into the night.

p179.s4.b4.q: but such victories are not won without the faith of the sincere love of truth.

p179.s4.b5: The text says that this whole supper was Jesus’ last appeal to the deserting Judas. Up to that very hour he had done everything possible to save him, just as he had for the others. But when love is once really dead, even the kindest warning usually only intensifies hatred and drives the person to carry out his selfish plans to the full. This insight shows how important it is to turn back before the heart hardens.
p179.s5.h: V. Establishing the Remembrance Supper — Freedom Left in Symbols
p179.s5.b0: Taking the third cup, the “⟦Q 179:5.1⟧cup of blessing,⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said it would be the cup of his remembrance, the cup of a new dispensation of grace and truth. Then he broke the bread, passed it around, and said that he was the bread of life. The old Passover commemorated the emergence from slavery into freedom; the new supper symbolizes the emergence from the bondage of ceremonialism and selfishness into the brotherhood of the liberated faith sons of God.

p179.s5.b2: The text explains that Jesus deliberately used symbols rather than precise definitions. He wanted to keep later generations from binding his teaching with the dead chains of tradition and dogma, and he did not want to cramp the believer’s spiritual imagination with a fixed form. Yet over the centuries people reduced these simple symbols to a set formula of almost mathematical precision. None of his teachings became more tradition-standardized.

p179.s5.b3.q: The remembrance supper is the believer’s symbolic rendezvous with Michael.

p179.s5.b4: The narrator also answers, briefly, the old debate about the Master’s presence at the supper. When those who are Son-believing and God-knowing partake, the Master is really present, so there is no need to attach to the symbols any puerile misinterpretations of that presence. When the believer becomes spirit-conscious, the Son’s spirit fraternizes with the indwelling fragment of the Father. What matters is not the bread and cup as objects, but the awakened spiritual consciousness of those who share them.

p179.s5.b5.q: This is the new Passover which I leave with you

p179.s5.b6: This great event took place in the upper room of a friend, without sacred form or ceremonial consecration, and without ecclesiastical sanction. Jesus told them that when they did this, they should first look back on his life in the flesh and then, by faith, look forward to the supper they would share in the eternal kingdom. Once more he urged them not to contend over who was greatest but to be as brethren. The company ended this bloodless Passover by singing the one hundred and eighteenth Psalm together.
p179.s6.b0: Paper 179 sets side by side the human craving for position, rising even on the most solemn night, and the Master kneeling in the midst of it. Jesus served before he rebuked, called the betrayer with love to the very end, and left even the way of remembering him in symbols, so as not to harm people’s spiritual freedom. In this paper the reader sees a faith in which service, freedom, and remembrance are woven together.

p179.s6.b2: In the next paper, Paper 180, “The Farewell Discourse,” Jesus leaves the eleven a new commandment and the promise of the Spirit of Truth.
p180.lead: The last teaching in the upper room: the new commandment, the vine and the branches, the enmity of the world, the promised helper, the Spirit of Truth, and why his leaving was for their good.

p180.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p180.s0.h: Introduction — Why He Had Them Sit Down Again
p180.s0.b0: After the supper ended with the singing of the Psalm, the apostles thought they would return straight to the camp. But Jesus had them sit down again. He reminded them that when he had once sent them out without purse or wallet, they had lacked nothing; now, in troublous times when they could no longer depend on the good will of the multitudes, they were to make provision for their own support.
p180.s0.b1: Then he said that the time had come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Soon they would seek him and not find him, but when they had finished their work on earth, they would come to him. This paper presents in six sections the farewell discourse that began this way. Its content is what the one who was leaving wanted, first and most deeply, to leave with those who would remain.

p180.s1.h: I. The New Commandment — Beyond Loving the Neighbor
p180.s1.b0: Jesus now gave the new commandment he had foreshadowed in the parable of the foot washing. The apostles knew well the commandment to love their neighbor as themselves. But the Master was not wholly satisfied with that. He changed the measure of love from “yourself” to “⟦Q 180:1.1⟧as I have loved you.⟦/Q⟧”

p180.s1.b1.q: That you love one another even as I have loved you. And by this will all men know that you are my disciples if you thus love one another.

p180.s1.b2: Jesus said this commandment was not a new burden but a new joy. Greater love has no man than to lay down his life for his friends, and the apostles were no longer servants but friends. The narrator adds an important comment: what Jesus demands is loyalty, not sacrifice, and the service of a friend for a friend can never be called a sacrifice.

p180.s1.b4.q: it does not create a new world, but it most certainly does make the old world new.

p180.s1.b5: The Master had taught the apostles that they were sons of God, then called them brethren, and now, before he left, he called them friends. This change of names traces the deepening of a relationship. Today’s reader, too, may find that when faith is seen not as a list of duties but as a friendship, the very same service turns from a burden into a joy.
p180.s2.h: II. The Vine and the Branches — The True Meaning of Prayer
p180.s2.b0: Jesus compared himself to the true vine, the Father to the husbandman, and the apostles to the branches. Just as a branch separated from the vine withers, so they could not yield the fruits of loving service unless they abode in him. The vine is pruned only to increase its fruitfulness. The apostles recalled the large emblem of the grape and vine at the entrance to Herod’s temple and the old teaching that the Messiah would be “⟦Q 180:2.3⟧a stem arising out of the vine⟦/Q⟧” of David’s ancestors.

p180.s2.b1.q: Herein is the Father glorified: that the vine has many living branches, and that every branch bears much fruit.

p180.s2.b2: The narrator points out that misunderstanding of what was said here about prayer later caused great sorrow. Believers came to regard prayer in Jesus’ name as a sort of supreme magic for getting anything they asked, and for centuries honest souls have wrecked their faith on this stumbling block. Prayer is not a process of getting your way but a program of taking God’s way. When one’s will is truly aligned with his, one can ask anything conceived by that will-union.

p180.s2.b3.q: When the branch of the vine is alive, there can be only one answer to all its petitions: increased grape bearing.

p180.s2.b4: This parable corrects our expectations of prayer. Even when a living branch asks for selfish ease, the divine answer is more and more bearing of the fruits of the spirit. The Father’s hand of discipline, too, is laid on in love for the sake of fruit, and a wise husbandman cuts away only the dead branches. When an answer to prayer does not take the shape we wanted, the reader may consider that it could be an answer aimed at more fruit.
p180.s3.h: III. Enmity of the World — The Way, the Truth, and the Life
p180.s3.b0: Jesus told them not to be discouraged if the world hated them; it had hated him first. They were in the world, but their lives were not to be worldlike; they were chosen out of the world to represent the spirit of another world to that very world. Those who had known the light and rejected it had no excuse, for the light that would save if accepted can only condemn if knowingly rejected.
p180.s3.b1: Yet he promised not to leave them alone. In the Father’s universe there are many tarrying-places, and he would go before them and send for them. When Thomas said they did not know the way, Jesus answered that he was the way; when Philip asked to be shown the Father, Jesus answered that he who had seen him had seen the Father.

p180.s3.b2.q: Thomas, I am the way, the truth, and the life. No man goes to the Father except through me.

p180.s4.h: IV. The Promised Helper — Leaving in Order to Be Nearer
p180.s4.b0: Jesus promised that after he went to the Father and received the final sovereignty of his domain, he would pour out the Spirit of Truth upon all flesh. Now he could be with them only in person, in one place; then he would be with all who desired his presence, wherever they were, and with each of them at the same time. That is why he said it was better for him to go away.

p180.s4.b1.q: Do you not discern that it is better for me to go away; that I leave you in the flesh so that I may the better and the more fully be with you in the spirit?

p180.s4.b2: In this new day the apostles would be indwelt by the Son as well as by the Father. The Spirit of Truth would guide and comfort them and bring to their remembrance all that the Master had taught. When Judas Alpheus, who seldom asked anything, made bold to put a question, Jesus smiled and answered that this spirit would live in the heart of each one and so draw all the children of light together. Judas did not fully understand, but he grasped the promise of the new teacher.
p180.s5.h: V. The Spirit of Truth — Living Truth and the Golden Rule
p180.s5.b0: In this section the narrator explains the nature of the Spirit of Truth. It is not the letter or law of truth but the conviction of truth, the consciousness and assurance of true meanings on real spirit levels. Truth can be known and lived, but it cannot be imprisoned in formulas or creeds. When humans undertake to formulate divine truth, it speedily dies.

p180.s5.b1.q: Static truth is dead truth, and only dead truth can be held as a theory.

head: Level
How the text defines it
rows: Intelligence

Truth

p180.s5.b3: The text takes the golden rule as its example. Read literally, it could lead someone to reason that because he wants others to speak their full minds to him, he should speak his full mind to them, a course that might bring no end of sorrow. People take the golden rule variously: as an intellectual affirmation, an emotional gratification, a social yardstick, or a moral injunction. But for the believer in the kingdom, it becomes a call so to relate oneself to others that they receive the highest possible good from that contact.
p180.s5.b4: Love works the same way. The text says that unselfish love must undergo a constant and living readaptation of relationships under the leading of the Spirit of Truth. Our concept of the highest good of the one we love keeps changing and enlarging, and love must take into account both the present evil environment and the eternal goal of divine destiny. Love is not to follow a fixed pattern set once and for all; as the other person grows, the shape of our love must grow too.
p180.s5.b5: The same principle applies to the teaching of nonresistance to evil. It is a spiritual pronouncement that combines nonresistance of all selfish reaction to the universe with the active pursuit of true spirit values. Neither the golden rule nor nonresistance can be rightly understood as dogma or precept; they can be comprehended only by living them in the living interpretation of the Spirit of Truth.

p180.s5.b6.q: The old religion taught self-sacrifice; the new religion teaches only self-forgetfulness, enhanced self-realization in conjoined social service and universe comprehension.

p180.s6.h: VI. The Necessity for Leaving — Sorrow Turned to Joy
p180.s6.b0: Jesus warned that the hour would come when those who killed them would think they were doing a service to God. He told them in advance so that, when the time came, they might be strengthened by knowing that he had known everything and that his spirit was with them. Surprised that none of them asked why he was leaving, he told them plainly, as one friend to another, that his going was for their good.

p180.s6.b1.q: I have yet much to say to you, but you cannot stand any more just now.

p180.s6.b2: Jesus said that the Spirit of Truth would not speak of himself but would declare what the Father had revealed to the Son. This spirit comes forth from the Son, reveals the Son’s truth, and glorifies the Son as the Son glorified the Father. Indwelling the believer, the spirit illuminates the difference between sin and righteousness and enables one to judge wisely in one’s own heart. The heart of this promise is that an inner discernment grows in place of external rules.
p180.s6.b3: He explained the meaning of the parting with the figure of a woman in travail. Her anguish is forgotten in the joy of the child’s birth. The apostles would grieve at first, but when they saw him again, their sorrow would be turned into a rejoicing no one could take from them. He had spoken to them in parables because they were children in the spirit; when they were perfected in spirit growth, they would see the Father himself. Yet the eleven still could not get away from their idea of a material kingdom to be set up on earth.
p180.s7.b0: Paper 180 shows what the last words of one who is leaving ought to be. Jesus left not rules but a measure of love; he promised not an institution but the living Spirit of Truth. He did not deny the sorrow of parting, yet he showed that it was the beginning of a deeper companionship. This paper moves faith from duty to friendship, and from form to living experience.

p181.lead: The last hour in the upper room: the promise of a peace the world cannot give, and a parting word spoken to each of the eleven as the Master went around the table.

p181.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p181.s0.h: Introduction — Hearing a Promise the Way We Want
p181.s0.b0: After the farewell discourse, Jesus visited informally with the apostles. At last it began to dawn on these Galileans that their Master was really going to leave them. Their hope grasped at the promise that he would be with them again after a little while, but they easily forgot that this return, too, would be only for a little while.
p181.s0.b1: The text pinpoints the reason sharply. Many took the promise to mean that the Master was going to the Father for a brief visit and would soon return to establish the kingdom, because that reading fit both their lifelong beliefs and their ardent hopes. This observation, that people readily find an interpretation that justifies their own longings, serves as a mirror for the reader of the whole paper.
p181.s1.h: I. Last Words of Comfort — A Peace the World Cannot Give
p181.s1.b0: Jesus said that while he was in the flesh he could be but one individual, but once delivered from mortal nature he could return as a spirit indweller of every believer. So the Son of Man would become a spiritual incarnation in the souls of all true believers. He would guide them not only through this life but through the many abodes of the heaven of heavens.

p181.s1.b1.q: Life in the Father’s eternal creation is not an endless rest of idleness and selfish ease but rather a ceaseless progression in grace, truth, and glory.

p181.s1.b2: He told them that to follow him they should not imitate the natural life he had been required to live in the flesh, but live according to the spirit of his teachings and the ideal of his life: doing the Father’s will. The distinction matters. Discipleship does not mean copying Jesus’ trade, dress, or way of living, but inheriting the devotion to the Father’s will that he carried.

p181.s1.b3.q: Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. I make these gifts not as the world gives—by measure—I give each of you all you will receive.

p181.s1.b4: He said that when persecution scattered them and they felt alone in the world, he would know of their isolation, just as they would know of his when they scattered and left the Son of Man in the hands of his enemies. Yet he was never alone; the Father was always with him. To be alone and yet not alone is the real shape of the peace he leaves. For those who receive the Spirit of Truth, it becomes a well of living water springing up into eternal life.

p181.s1.b5.q: In this world you will have tribulation, but be of good cheer; I have triumphed in the world and shown you the way to eternal joy and everlasting service.

p181.s1.b6: The narrator explains this peace by contrasting it with two kinds of worldly comfort. All that unbelieving materialists can hope for is stoicism, which resolves to endure the worst, or optimism, which longs for a peace that never really comes. Both are of some use in earthly life, but neither has anything to do with the peace Jesus gives.

p181.s1.b8: Jesus was thoroughly devoted to his mission, yet he was not an unfeeling stoic; he always looked for the cheerful side of life, yet he was not a blind optimist. He knew all that was to befall him, and he was unafraid. His peace is the assurance of a son who fully believes that his career for time and eternity is safely in the keeping of an all-wise, all-loving, and all-powerful spirit Father. It passes the understanding of the mortal mind, but the believing heart can enjoy it to the full.
p181.s2.h: II. Farewell Personal Admonitions (1) — John, Simon Zelotes, and Matthew
p181.s2.b0: Having finished his admonitions to the group, Jesus went around the table and spoke to each one in turn, and each man rose as the Master addressed him. The scene shows that the Master knew and loved the eleven not only as a group but as individuals, each with a different temperament, weakness, and mission.
p181.s2.b1: To John, the youngest, he entrusted the care of his earthly family, since John would very likely outlive the others. To the “son of thunder” who once wanted fire called down on unbelievers, he said that he should become the apostle of the new commandment. When John asked how he could learn to love his brethren more, Jesus answered that he would learn it when he first loved their Father in heaven more and became truly interested in their welfare.

p181.s2.b2.q: And all such human interest is fostered by understanding sympathy, unselfish service, and unstinted forgiveness.

p181.s2.b3: Jesus paused for a moment with a sad countenance beside Judas’s empty seat, but no one except possibly Andrew guessed its meaning. To Simon Zelotes, the fiery patriot, he said that he did not doubt his loyalty, but that Simon was still set on making the kingdom come according to his own liking. No one would be more disheartened after the Master’s departure. Yet he would always be the Master’s apostle, and he was promised that the Master would be with him through all his season of discouragement.

p181.s2.b4.q: once more I warn you that they who fight with the sword perish with the sword, while they who labor in the spirit achieve life everlasting in the kingdom to come with joy and peace in the kingdom which now is.

p181.s2.b5: To Matthew, the former publican, Jesus said that he knew of his anxieties and labors to keep the treasury replenished, which his brethren did not know. The apostles would soon be scattered and go out alone to the ends of the earth, and Andrew would no longer direct them. Matthew’s mission was to show the world what the Father could do for a hated tax-gatherer, and to dedicate his life to showing that God is no respecter of persons.
p181.s3.h: II. Farewell Personal Admonitions (2) — The Other Eight
p181.s3.b0: To James he said that true wisdom embraces discretion as well as courage, and sagacity along with aggressiveness. There would come supreme moments when his disciples must lay down their lives, but in ordinary circumstances it would be far better to placate the wrath of unbelievers and live long to win souls. Andrew he commended for his fair leadership and released from responsibility as administrative head. Yet his moral responsibility to hold his brethren together with a loving hand in the trying time ahead remained.

p181.s3.b1.q: Our kingdom is a realm of order, and where two or more will creatures act in co-operation, there is always provided the authority of leadership.

p181.s3.b2: The last charge to Andrew brings out the worth of an unseen place. If his brethren wished, he was to promote peace and harmony among the groups of believers and show impartial love to the Greeks in the West and to Abner in the East. Though the great works seen by men might not fall to him, he was to be content to be the teacher and counselor of those who did them. These words comfort all who serve behind the scenes.

p181.s3.b4: To the Alpheus twins Jesus said not to be discouraged when there were no multitudes to manage. They would show how cheerfully and courageously a person called for a season to God’s special service can return to the labors of former days. At the heart of this charge is the realization that to one who knows God there is no such thing as common labor or secular toil.

p181.s3.b5.q: To you who have worked with me, all things have become sacred, and all earthly labor has become a service even to God the Father.

p181.s3.b6: To Philip he first read aloud the last question in his heart: what would he ever do if the Master went away? The world, Jesus said, is full of people who look at life as Philip did, so he had a great mission. To Nathaniel he said that the expression of even a good thought must be adjusted to the state of the hearer. When Nathaniel confessed that he could not understand the full meaning of the teaching, Jesus answered that he must now learn from the master of all teachers, actual experience.

p181.s3.b7.q: Sincerity is most serviceable in the work of the kingdom when it is wedded to discretion.

p181.s3.b8.q: what you have not been able to get from my teachings and my life, you must now prepare to acquire at the hand of that master of all teachers—actual experience.

p181.s3.b9: To Thomas he said that his doubts had perplexed his brethren but had never troubled the Master. Last of all, he told Peter he was distressed that Peter had not learned to think before he spoke. When Peter declared that even if all the others stumbled he would die for the Master, Jesus foretold that before the cock crowed that night Peter would deny him three or four times. What he had failed to learn in peaceful association, he would learn through much trouble and many sorrows.
p181.s3.b10: Jesus told all the apostles not to be dismayed that they could not grasp the full meaning of the gospel, for they were finite mortals and what he had taught was infinite and eternal. He promised again that when he was raised up he would tarry with them for a season, and he told them he loved them with the love wherewith the Father loved him. Then they sang a hymn and left for the camp on the Mount of Olives.
p181.s4.b0: Paper 181 records how the departing Master left peace to the whole group and a word meant only for each one. He did not cover up their weaknesses but named them honestly, while making clear that those weaknesses did not lessen his affection in the least. Reading the eleven admonitions in turn, the reader finds himself standing in the place of the apostle nearest his own temperament and hearing the word meant for him.
